printed_headline_estimate: Table 3 (PDF p. 7 / p. 81), binary logistic regression for water poverty (income commitment > 3% in lifeline block, Nagelkerke R2 = 0.190, exact regression N not reported in main text): demographic/socioeconomic predictors only, e.g., Female head OR = 2.78 (95% CI 2.52–3.07, p < 0.001), Brown race/color OR = 2.84 (95% CI 1.45–5.42, p = 0.002), Higher Education OR = 0.12 (95% CI 0.07–0.20, p < 0.001), Children OR = 1.49 (95% CI 1.38–1.60, p < 0.001); tariff/subsidy evaluations in Tables 1–2 (PDF pp. 5–6, Omega = 0.60–1.82; lifeline income share 0.45% in 2019 vs. 0.41% in 2020 across 1,141,984 total units) are purely descriptive without SEs, CIs, or p-values.

rationale: The paper contains two empirical components, neither of which yields an inferential SWiM-eligible governance/tariff effect. First, the evaluation of the increasing block tariff (IBT) structure, subsidy regressivity (Komives et al. Omega index in Table 1, PDF p. 5), social tariff coverage and >3% income-commitment shares across income groups (Table 2, PDF p. 6), and the 2019 vs. 2020/2021 tariff restructuring (0.45% vs. 0.41% average income share, PDF p. 5) is purely descriptive/accounting with zero standard errors, confidence intervals, test statistics, or p-values. Second, the sole inferential statistical model in the paper—a binary logistic regression predicting household water poverty (>3% income commitment in the lifeline block; Table 3, PDF p. 7)—includes exclusively demographic and socioeconomic covariates (head's gender, race/color, marital status, schooling, household size, elderly presence, and children presence) and tests no legal, tariff, subsidy, tenure, or institutional exposure, thus failing narrow Criterion 2.
